newsitem.title: USA: Morgan buying mutual fund firm stake for $900 million.
newsitem.headline: Morgan buying mutual fund firm stake for $900 million.

text.p: J.P. Morgan & Co. said Wednesday it agreed to pay $900 million for a 45 percent stake in American Century Cos., the nation's fourth-largest mutual fund company, in a bid to expand its financial services business.
Morgan, the nation's fourth largest bank, said the two companies would form a new partnership to market pension plans such as 401(k) plans to corporations and individual investors.
Industry analysts said the move would put Morgan into a new business, catering to consumers, and probably make its investment management business more profitable as well.

"It's interesting to see that Morgan, which has catered to a highly affluent and essentially almost an institutional marketplace is now recognising the tremendous profitability of the retail side of the business," said Burton Greenwald, a mutual fund consultant in Philadelphia.
He said Morgan's strong reputation and expertise overseas would match up well with the strong domestic retail business of American Century to create an "even more powerful factor in the business."
One area the combined company wants to develop is selling investments plans to corporations for their employee retirement plans, one of the fastest-growing areas in financial services, analysts said.
The growth prospects of that business helped drive the $11 billion merger of Morgan Stanley & Co. Inc. and Dean Witter Discover & Co. earlier this year.
Morgan said the purchase of the American Century stake will give it retail mutual fund distribution, products and technology that complement its traditional focus on institutional investors.
Morgan, which is based in New York, also said it plans to offer financial services to individuals, focusing on the wealthy.

American Century, a no-load mutual fund company, sells directly to individuals, manages $60 billion in assets in about 70 mutual funds. Morgan manages $234 billion, about 10 percent of it in mutual funds.
Morgan Chairman Douglas Warner III said the partnership will accelerate the company's asset management business by adding service and product expertise, distribution and technology.

American Century President William Lyons said Morgan has an option to raise its stake to 50 percent. But he said Morgan was not seeking to acquire control and that the founding Stowers family would still have control if its stake were 50 percent.
"Morgan's desire is to keep American Century independent," Lyons said in an interview, adding Morgan was looking for a partner to help it service large institutional clients.

Lyons said that Morgan, a New York financial powerhouse with roots dating to 1838, and American Century, based in Kansas City, Mo., had similar cultures despite some differences. Both firms put customers first and take a "team-oriented" approach rather than relying on star managers, he said.
Morgan also said that two Morgan executives, Ramon de Oliveira and Edward Kelly III, will join American Century's board of directors. The companies expect the deal to close in four to six months.
Morgan stock rose $1.44 to $115.69 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
